references.text: The context of the wedding at Cana: [ref:Joh 2:1-2|John 2:1-2] tells us that Jesus and his disciples were invited to a wedding, and it is in this situation that the wine runs out and Jesus' mother turns to him.

Jesus' response to his mother and her further instruction to the servants: [ref:Joh 2:4-5|John 2:4-5] shows that Mary had confidence that Jesus could do something about the situation, even after his seemingly dismissive reply.
The result of Mary's appeal: [ref:Joh 2:7-9|John 2:7-9] shows that Jesus actually intervened and turned water into wine – his first sign.

Mary's faithful attitude is already shown at the Annunciation in [ref:Luk 1:38|Luke 1:38], where she says "Behold, I am the Lord's servant". This trust also characterizes her appeal to Jesus when the wine runs out at Cana.

[ref:Luk 2:19|Luke 2:19] tells us that Mary treasured all these things in her heart and pondered them. Her knowledge of Jesus' identity and calling lies behind her appeal to him when the wine runs out.
[ref:Luk 2:51|Luke 2:51] again confirms Mary's habit of keeping events and words in her heart, which explains her expectation that Jesus could help in a difficult situation.

The second time in the Gospel of John where Jesus' mother plays a prominent role is at the cross in [ref:Joh 19:26-27|John 19:26-27]. Both times she is referred to as "Jesus' mother" without being named.

[ref:Jes 55:1|Isaiah 55:1] invites all who are thirsty to come and receive wine and milk without payment. The lack of wine at Cana and Jesus' miraculous provision point toward the abundance of God's kingdom as promised by the prophets.

[ref:Am 9:13-14|Amos 9:13-14] prophesies a messianic time of abundant wine, where "the mountains shall drip sweet wine". Jesus' miracle of turning water into wine can be seen as a fulfillment of this messianic expectation.
